transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I’m here because I can’t stop noticing how crooked and swollen one side of my face looks in the lesson videos. Once I see it, I just think the students, their parents, and the staff must be staring at that instead of listening to me.
Do you think it’s possible that your face looks more normal than it seems to you?
I don’t know. When I see the lesson videos, that side just looks crooked and swollen to me. It’s hard to believe other people aren’t noticing it too, especially the students and parents.
Are you certain that one side of your face is actually crooked and swollen?

I feel certain when I see the lesson videos. That side looks crooked and swollen to me, and I can’t stop focusing on it. It makes me think everyone watching is looking at that instead of hearing what I’m saying.
Do you think you might be mistaken about how abnormal that side of your face looks?

I mean, I suppose I could be, but when I see myself in the lesson videos it looks so obvious. That side of my face looks crooked and swollen, and I can’t get past the feeling that the students, parents, and staff are all staring at it instead of listening to me.
Do you find yourself repeatedly checking your face in mirrors or videos because of this?

Yes. Before I post a recorded lesson or join a parent conference, I keep checking the camera angle and replaying clips. I’ll cover part of my face with my hand to see if it looks better, and sometimes I re-record the whole lesson over and over. It takes so long that I miss prep work and end up late for class.
If you were alone and no one else would ever see the video, would your face still upset you this much?

Yes, I think so. Even if nobody else saw it, I’d still fixate on that side of my face looking crooked and swollen. But knowing students or parents might see it makes me feel even worse, like they’ll be staring at my face instead of listening to me.
When thoughts about that side of your face come up, do you try to resist or push those thoughts away?
I’m not sure I really try to push them away. I mostly get pulled into looking at it and trying to figure out whether it’s as bad as it seems.
Outside of concerns about your face, do you usually fear being judged or embarrassed in social situations?
I’m not sure. I mean, I don’t generally think about being embarrassed in every social situation. It’s more when I’m worried people can see my face.
Do these thoughts about your face ever feel unwanted and senseless to you, like they intrude into your mind even though you know they don’t really make sense?

They do feel like they just take over once I notice that side of my face. I keep seeing it as crooked and swollen on the videos, and then I can’t stop thinking that the students, parents, or staff are looking at that instead of listening to me.
Has anyone told you that your face looks normal or that the crooked, swollen look is much less noticeable than you think?

People have tried to reassure me, but when I see the lesson videos, I still see that side as crooked and swollen. Then I just think the students, parents, and staff must be focused on it instead of what I’m saying.
Are you mainly afraid that people will judge you because of how your face looks?
Yes. When I see the lesson videos and notice that side of my face looking crooked and swollen, I feel like everyone—students, parents, staff—is staring at it and not listening to what I’m saying.
Is the main thing upsetting you that there is something wrong with how your face looks?

Yes. It’s that side of my face—I see it as crooked and swollen in the lesson videos, and I can’t stop focusing on it. Then I feel like the students, parents, and staff must be staring at it instead of hearing what I’m saying.
If you felt sure your face looked completely normal, would you still be afraid in those situations?

No, I don’t think so. If I could look at the videos and feel sure that side of my face looked normal, I wouldn’t be so worried about the students, parents, and staff staring at me instead of listening.
Apart from your face, do you have a strong fear of being watched or judged in social situations?
I’m not sure. I mostly notice the fear when it’s about my face.
Do you spend a lot of time trying to hide or fix that side of your face?

Yes. Before I post a lesson recording or join a parent conference, I keep adjusting the camera angle and replaying the clips over and over. I’ll hold my hand over part of my face sometimes, or just re-record the whole lesson repeatedly. It takes so long that I miss preparation work and end up late for classes.
Are these repeated checking and re-recording rituals only about how that side of your face looks?

Yes. It’s really about that side of my face—trying to make sure it doesn’t look wrong on camera. I keep changing the angle, replaying the clips, sometimes covering part of my face or recording it again. It can go on so long that I miss my prep time and end up late for class.
Are you also very worried about any other part of your body or health, besides that side of your face?
No, not really. It’s mainly that side of my face that I get stuck on.
Do other people generally say that the side of your face looks normal or only slightly different?
They might say it looks normal, but I can’t see it that way. On the lesson videos it looks crooked and swollen to me, and I feel like everyone must be staring at that side instead of listening to me.
Do you have any other repeated unwanted thoughts or rituals that are not about how your face looks?
No, I haven’t noticed other thoughts or rituals like that. It’s really just the stuff about my face.
Do you ever avoid being seen by other people because of how your face looks?

Yeah. Before a recorded lesson or a parent conference, I’ll keep adjusting the camera angle and replaying clips. I sometimes hold my hand over that side of my face, or re-record the whole thing over and over. It can take so long that I miss prep work and end up late for class.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient is preoccupied with a perceived defect in appearance (one side of the face seen as 'crooked and swollen') despite reassurance that it looks normal or only slightly different. The concern is appearance-focused rather than a general fear of scrutiny, and it is accompanied by repetitive behaviors such as mirror/video checking, camouflaging, camera-angle adjustment, and repeated re-recording. This causes significant functional impairment at work. Social anxiety was considered, but the fear is contingent on the perceived facial defect and would remit if the patient felt the face looked normal. OCD was considered, but the obsessions/compulsions are restricted to appearance concerns, supporting body dysmorphic disorder under hypochondriacal disorder in ICD-10.
